title: Reference placement manifest
$comment: A protocol that never settles still has to say WHERE the lcp: reference rides, so a stranger can find it. This is the non-settling sibling of binding/profile.schema.json — no rail, no WLD-3 recovery triple, no indexing, no finality, no lifecycle: none of those mean anything without a settlement, and a manifest carrying them with hollow values would declare properties nobody can check.

container.$comment: Hoisted so `readAlso[].container` references the SAME definition rather than a second copy. A duplicated closed set is a set that drifts, and the repo's convention is to guard duplicated enums with a test — cheaper to have one definition. Internal $ref is same-document, so the runner's inline-schema validator resolves it (verified against @cfworker/json-schema).

segments.description: OPTIONAL — the exact key sequence the walker takes, overriding the dot-split of `field`. Needed when a KEY contains literal dots: UCP capability keys follow [reverse-domain].{service}.{capability}, so com.integraledger.legal_context is ONE key under `extensions`. When present, `field` is documentation for humans and this is the machine-readable form — the same division tagged-array uses.

oneOf.description: The path resolves directly to the slot. ACP, A2A, AP2, ACK, MPP, x402.

constants.description: OPTIONAL — sibling fields written onto a NEWLY CREATED entry because the HOST's schema requires them, never applied when merging into an entry that already exists (a counterparty's own prose is theirs). UCP is the consumer: policies[] entries are required:[type,description], so an entry carrying only a tag and a value is an invalid document, and a writer emitting one would assert a shape the host rejects. A constant may not name the entry's own tagField or valueField — assertManifestHygiene refuses that, because a manifest declaring a constant the writer would drop is stating something it does not mean.

termsUrlField.description: OPTIONAL — the entry property carrying the human-readable terms URL, where the host declares the locator on the SAME entry as the reference. Container-relative because the entry's index is chosen at write time (replace-by-tag, else append), so no dotted path in termsUrlFields can name it. UCP is the consumer: its policy object is additionalProperties:true and declares `url` ("Optional link to the full policy document", format uri), and LCP v1.38 §C.3's illustration carries url and atrHash side by side in one entry. Written on create AND on merge, unlike constants — the URL is half of our own advertisement on our own tagged entry, not a host sibling. May not name the entry's own tagField or valueField.

oneOf.description: An array of entries; find the entry whose tagField equals tag; the reference lives in valueField. UCP (links / type=terms_of_service / url) and Mastercard VI (constraints / type=<ns>.lcp_terms_hash / value) reduce to the SAME rule with different data — two protocols with nothing else in common sharing one rule is the evidence the abstraction is discovered rather than invented.
Case-insensitive key equality per RFC 9110. Visa TAP.

writeCondition.$comment: Hoisted for the same reason `container` is: the manifest and each alias reference the SAME definition, so the gate cannot drift into a looser second copy. ACP makes an otherwise-conformant write non-conformant depending on the document in hand: CheckoutSessionBase is additionalProperties:false, and what authorizes a top-level legal_context is a declaration at capabilities.extensions[] whose `extends` names $.CheckoutSession.legal_context, so the gate reads the authorization for the field it is about to write. Neither tier, pattern nor carrierClass expresses this: all three describe a carrier's standing in the abstract, and this describes one document. Note what the gate does NOT claim — it reads the session a seller composed, not the agent's request, so it cannot verify a declaration was itself negotiated; that obligation sits upstream of placement. Four of the five authoring rules live here and are mirrored in binding-core's assertManifestHygiene, which catches manifests authored in TypeScript; the fifth — a tagged-array gate reading its own tagField must list `container.tag` in `permits`, since that is then the only value the reader can return — has no schema half because JSON Schema cannot compare two sibling values.

path.description: The locator of the value that decides — human-readable, with `container` carrying the machine-readable form, the same division of labour `field` uses.

container.description: REQUIRED, and never inherited from the manifest. ACP's gate sits in a DIFFERENT container kind than either carrier it guards: it searches capabilities.extensions[] by tagged array, while the declared-extension placement's `legal_context` and placement-acp's alias beside `metadata.legal_context` are both object-paths. A default would be wrong on both, and would read the wrong place rather than read nothing.

permits.description: The values at `path` that PERMIT the write. An ALLOW-list because the values a gate must refuse cannot be enumerated — a session's active-extension list may carry any third party's identifier, so a deny-list would have to name everything and would fail open on the first value nobody thought of. A SET rather than a single string because a gate resolving through object-path compares a scalar, where presence alone would fail open — and Mastercard VI needs two of them, the two vct values whose credential type carries a constraints array at all, where ACP's tagged-array gate is the degenerate single-value case. Absent, non-string and unlisted values all decline the write.

and.$comment: A GATE IS A CONJUNCTION, and ACP is why. An extension declaration authorizes a field on the ONE schema its `extends` target names — ACP's core `discount` extension enumerates $.CheckoutSessionCreateRequest.discounts, $.CheckoutSessionUpdateRequest.discounts and $.CheckoutSession.discounts as three separate targets — while `Capabilities` is ONE definition shared by request and response whose `extensions` oneOf is undiscriminated. So a schema-valid CheckoutSessionCreateRequest may carry declaration OBJECTS, and an identifier-only gate would write a top-level field into a document that is additionalProperties:false and names it nowhere: measured against the live schema, a valid create request in and an invalid one out. Items reference this SAME definition so a term cannot drift into a looser shape, and `not: {required: [and]}` holds depth at exactly two — a nested gate is an expression language, and a manifest that needs one has stopped being data. binding-core's assertManifestHygiene holds the two rules JSON Schema cannot: terms must not repeat a `path`, since the looser copy would silently decide the gate.
and.description: OPTIONAL — further terms, ALL of which must hold. A conjunction and never a disjunction: each term names an independent fact that must be true of the document, and an OR over facts passes on the weakest of them. ACP's declared-extension carrier is the consumer — its second term reads `status`, REQUIRED on CheckoutSessionBase, absent from every request schema in the live spec, and a closed eleven-value enum, so it is the host's own evidence that the document in hand is the CheckoutSession the declaration extends.

allOf.$comment: LCP §8.3.6 states Protocol Extension is Tier B BY DEFINITION — it means the host protocol's own verification and settlement procedure is atrHash-aware, which no host has agreed to, so stock implementations reject the extended variant. A manifest claiming both is internally inconsistent and is rejected here rather than in prose. Note the converse is NOT asserted: a Tier B placement need not be a protocol-extension, and a strong Tier A carrier riding a host's own extensions framework is http-advisory, not protocol-extension, because the host still does nothing with the hash.

A bare value carries no type tag, so the field's contract must fix the type unambiguously. More than one permitted carrierType under bare-value means a reader cannot tell a sha256 from a url — the manifest would be declaring an unresolvable field.

The REFERENCE field must be able to hold an integrity-bearing carrier — sha256, ipfs and ar are content-addressed; url only locates a document and commits to nothing about its content. A manifest whose reference field permits only `url` is declaring discovery and calling it a placement, which is precisely the weakest-available-reading failure this branch exists to stop. THE RULE STANDS ON ITS OWN REASONING, not on a citation: a url locates a document and commits to nothing about its content, so a reference field that can hold only a url cannot support any claim the record makes about the terms — it is discovery wearing a placement's name. LCP v1.38 §C.2 agrees ('A terms-of-use policy page is not a per-transaction terms record and is not a substitute for one') but states it as a description rather than a prohibition; v1.37's wording was 'MUST NOT be substituted for one', and this comment quoted that as the ground until 2026-08-08. It is now support, not the ground — the enforcement here does not depend on which way the appendix words it. A protocol's discovery carrier is declared as `termsUrlFields`, or as a readAlso alias with carrierClass `discovery` — never as the reference field itself.

protocol.description: The commerce protocol this placement describes. The enum is INLINED from vocabulary/protocol-id.schema.json rather than $ref'd — the runner passes schemas inline and the subject's validator has no file resolver for a relative external ref — and a package test guards this copy against that file.

pattern.description: The LCP §8.3 pattern subset a non-settling protocol can exhibit. native-field, id-reuse and overlay-contract are SETTLEMENT patterns and are excluded by construction — a placement has no settlement to bind into.

tier.description: LCP §8.3 wire compatibility. A = works today against stock implementations, no upstream coordination. B = requires a coordinated change to the host protocol's specification. Required, because a placement that cannot state which it is will be read as available when it is not. NOTE the axis is deliberately coarse: it does NOT separate a protocol's strong Tier A carrier from its weak one — both ACP's declared extension and its metadata fallback are Tier A. That separation is carrier strength, declared per carrier, not per manifest.
tier.$comment: v1.37 §C.3 corrected an earlier reading that placed UCP's vendor capability at Tier B. UCP requires no central registry and no maintainer approval for a capability under a reverse-domain namespace the author controls, so the hash-bearing carrier is Tier A and available today. What replaces registration is authority binding, not approval. (Re-read against v1.38 on 2026-08-12: v1.38 §C.3 records `policies[]` as a Tier A carrier in the negotiated baseline.)

field.description: The LOCATOR a stranger uses to find the reference. For an object-path container it is a dotted path (metadata.legal_context). For a tagged array it reads links[type=terms_of_service].url — that form is documentation for humans, and `container` carries the machine-readable version. For a header map the LAST segment is the header name. Before `container` existed this property meant a resolvable path on six protocols and a bare CONTAINER NAME on two (UCP's `links`, Mastercard VI's `constraints`), so a stranger reading it found an array and no rule for searching it — the declared property was not the declared thing.

encoding.description: How the reference SITS in the declared field. `lcp-string` = the canonical `lcp:{type}:{value}` string. `reference-object` = the LCP §8.1 `{type, value}` object. `bare-value` = the raw value alone, with its type implied by the field's own contract (x402's `extra.atrHash`, MPP's `methodDetails.atrHash`, a UCP terms URL). REQUIRED: the host protocol decides this, not us, and writing the wrong shape produces a field no counterparty recognizes.

container.description: How the declared field is REACHED inside a host document. A closed set of three, derived from the ten protocols rather than imagined. Required: without it a tagged-array manifest could only name its container, defeating the reason the manifest exists.

writeCondition.description: OPTIONAL — the condition under which writing `field` is valid at all. Unmet, `place` REFUSES <protocol>/write-condition-unmet: the reference field IS the placement, so a document we may not write it into is a document nothing was placed in. Omitted means unconditional, which is what every carrier but ACP's top-level legal_context is — the axis does not change the behaviour of a manifest that does not declare it.

allOf.$comment: A condition gates a WRITE. On an alias that is never written it guards nothing while reading as a guard, which is worse than absent: a reviewer infers the carrier is conditional when in fact it never lands at all. binding-core's assertManifestHygiene rejects the same pairing, because a manifest authored in TypeScript never meets this schema.

writeCondition.description: OPTIONAL — the condition under which THIS alias's write is valid. Unmet, the alias is not written and the placement stands: an alias is an addition, and the reference already landed in `field`. That asymmetry with the manifest-level property is one rule, not two — a carrier whose condition is unmet is not written, and what that means depends on whether the carrier IS the placement. ACP is why the alias half must not refuse: its metadata carrier needs nothing from the counterparty, so refusing would mean no legal context could be recorded against any counterparty that has not adopted the extensions framework.

container.description: OPTIONAL — the container this alias resolves through, defaulting to the manifest's. Needed because a protocol's carriers are not always the same SHAPE of thing: UCP's canonical capability is an object-path at extensions.<reverse-domain>.legal-context while its discovery carrier is a tagged-array at links[type=terms_of_service].url. An alias already declares its own `encoding`; declaring where it sits is the same kind of fact one level further out.

readAlso.description: OPTIONAL — additional field paths `extract` also accepts, declared as DATA so no accepted shape is a silent convention. Each entry may carry its OWN `encoding`, defaulting to the manifest's: an alias frequently differs in shape from the canonical slot — ACP's canonical field holds an `lcp:` string while its Appendix-C alias holds a §8.1 object, and x402's canonical `extensions` slot holds an object while its `extra.atrHash` alias holds a bare hash. `bareType` fixes the type for a `bare-value` alias, since a bare value carries no type tag. `carrierClass` defaults to `integrity`; `discovery` marks a carrier that only LOCATES the terms document and commits to nothing about its content, and a discovery hit is reported as such so it can never be mistaken for an integrity read. `write` defaults to false — strict write — and `true` means `place` populates this carrier as well as `field`, which is what UCP §C.3 advises for a capability that may be silently pruned from the negotiated intersection.
readAlso.$comment: An entry is an OBJECT, not a bare string. A string[] would silently assume every alias has the canonical field's shape, and neither of the two protocols we can check against actually does — it would force each adapter to hard-code its alias decoding, putting the shape back into code, which is what declaring it as data was for. The rule 'readAlso may not repeat field' is NOT expressible in draft 2020-12 without $data — it compares two properties of the same object — so it is enforced by assertManifestHygiene in binding-core, which every placement package's manifest test calls. Do not assume the schema catches it.

termsUrlFields.description: OPTIONAL — the dotted paths of EVERY field carrying the human-readable terms URL, where the protocol has room for one. All slots are written by `place` and all are read and reconciled by `extract`, which refuses disagreement. A LIST because the predecessor member was singular and that was a measured defect twice over: x402's wire carries the URL in two places (accepts[].extra per §C.4's illustration, extensions…info per the authority schema), so a singular declaration could only name one — and no write path existed at all, so a seller assembling from published parts emitted a challenge the published buyer refuses (integra-protocol#8). Absent means this protocol carries no terms URL and a parser must not demand one; declared, the kit REQUIRES the URL of any integrity-bearing advertisement. Entries must be distinct from `field` and from every readAlso path — binding-core's assertManifestHygiene holds those cross-member rules, which JSON Schema cannot express without $data.

carrierTypes.description: Which binding-core carrier types this field can legally hold. A field with a tight length budget may accept only the shortest forms. Widening is a vector amendment, never a code-side default.

specRef.description: Citation for the protocol's own spec section that owns this field.
